newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Prince Charles bids to overcome unpopularity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Prince Charles bids to overcome unpopularity.

text.p: If Prince Charles had any illusions about his unpopularity, they were dispelled by 3,000 people at a television debate on the monarchy's future last week.
Asked whether Charles should succeed his mother Queen Elizabeth to the throne, the vast majority lifted red cards to show they opposed the idea.
Critics dismissed the rowdy debate as shambolic and meaningless, but the message struck home.

Less than 24 hours later, Buckingham Palace announced a five-year plan to restore the prince's standing, battered by his acrimonous divorce from Princess Diana and his confession of an extra-marital affair with Camilla Parker-Bowles.

Royal aides are frustrated that the public seems to be ignoring the prince's good works, in particular the Prince's Trust organisation which runs schemes to help around 50,000 disadvantaged youngsters a year.

"The public clearly does not understand all he has done and will do in the public domain and we are trying to do something about that," said trust chief executive Tom Shebbeare, one of the prince's closest aides.
"I think that what should be done is more of the same and a better job of explaining to the public what the Prince of Wales has achieved," he told a television interviewer.

Charles, widely regarded as a distant and somewhat prickly character, has none of the instinctive flair for publicity that helped Diana win the battle for the public's affections during their protracted and bitter divorce.
ECLIPSED BY DIANA

While she dominated the headlines this week with a high-profile visit to war-torn Angola, Charles picked up the crumbs with a speech on the importance of national study support centres in helping the young.

Charles runs a model village in southern England where he experiments with environmentally friendly farming techniques and he has firm views on modern architecture. But these will always be eclipsed by pictures of Diana in a low-cut dress.
His admission that he sometimes talked to plants and his interest in eastern religions has led many to label him "wacky".

Shebbeare blames the media for Charles' poor image with his fellow Britons. "I wonder if you'll be reporting on those things (Charles's meetings with world leaders) as much as you report on some of the other issues which I would describe quite often as more tittle-tattle than real work," he snapped.

A poll released last week in conjunction with the televised debate showed 34 percent of respondents thought Charles had done more than anyone else to damage the monarchy's image while only 11 percent blamed Diana. Just under half thought he would make a good king while 36 percent disagreed.
DOUBTS OVER ATTEMPT TO RESTORE IMAGE
The prince's team will try to repair the damage by boosting knowledge of his good works rather than attempting to change his image. But some commentators fear the effort might be too late.

"For Prince Charles, the task of restoring himself to public favour is so daunting as to appear, in some eyes, a mission impossible...Some believe that without more radical action, attempts to rehabilitate him may prove hopeless," said the Sunday Times newspaper.

"He is widely perceived as having blamed everyone else but himself for the public's failure to warm to his contribution on issues such as architecture and the environment, about which he feels passionately, let alone his more idiosyncratic interests in philosophy and eastern religion."
The Prince's aides stress they are taking a long-term view since the queen is likely to remain on the throne for some time to come, but there have already been signs of movement.

Newspapers said Diana and Charles had agreed to develop closer working ties to protect the monarchy for their two young sons and might carry out joint engagements later in the year, something which would have been unthinkable a few months ago.

And no effort seems too small. Charles has often displayed all the friendliness of a caged rat when cornered by the press on his frequent skiing holidays in Switzerland, but last week reporters found him more than ready to pose for them.
The smiles might have a deeper purpose. At the official opening of the new British Embassy in Tashkent last year, the prince was complemented on his sense of humour by the Uzbek prime minister.
"You are very generous," Charles replied. "I find it's the only way to avoid a nervous breakdown."
